\chapter{The Strong Preterites}
\label{ch:spanish-preterito-fuerte}
\hlchaptermodality{51}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can use tuve, hice and estuve, and hear that their stress sits on the stem.}

Latin's own perfect, carried through on verbs too heavily used to be rebuilt.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[tuve]{tuve — let the strong stem carry the stress}

\label{lesson:ES-C15-tener-preterite}



\begin{quote}
You know present \textbf{tengo, tienes, tiene}. Its completed past changes the stem to \textbf{tuv-} and uses \textbf{tuve, tuviste, tuvo}. Unlike \textbf{comí} and \textbf{comió}, none of these three forms carries a written accent.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: one strong singular pattern}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{person} & \textbf{present} & \textbf{completed past} \\
\midrule
yo & \textbf{tengo} & \textbf{tuve} \\
tú & \textbf{tienes} & \textbf{tuviste} \\
él / ella / usted & \textbf{tiene} & \textbf{tuvo} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The strong stem \textbf{tuv-} takes \textbf{-e, -iste, -o}. Say \textbf{tuve · tuviste · tuvo}. Stress remains in the stem, so normal spelling needs no accent mark. Reuse known \textbf{café}:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{Tuve café.} — “I had coffee.”
  \item \textbf{¿Tuviste café?} — “Did you have coffee?”
  \item \textbf{Tuvo café.} — “He, she, or you-formal had coffee.”
\end{itemize}

“Strong” describes the stem-stressed historical pattern. It does not mean that the meaning is forceful. Plural endings wait.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{Tener} continues Latin \textbf{tenēre}. Its past also belongs to an older strong history associated with Latin \textbf{tenuī}. Spanish sound change and analogy reshaped that material into the \textbf{tuv-} family. \textbf{Tenuī $\to$ tuve} is therefore a historical relationship, not a promise that every letter passed across intact.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item “tuve, tuviste, tuvo”
  \item “Tuve café.”
  \item “comí has final stress; tuve has stem stress”
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give the three learned \textbf{tener} forms. (\emph{Tuve, tuviste, tuvo.}) Which endings attach to \textbf{tuv-}? (\emph{-e, -iste, -o.}) Why are there no written accents? (The strong stem carries the stress.) What shaped \textbf{tuve} historically? (Older strong-perfect material, sound change, and analogy.) Next: reuse the strong endings with \textbf{hacer}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[hice]{hice — the strong pattern with one third-person swerve}

\label{lesson:ES-C15-hacer-preterite}



\begin{quote}
You know present \textbf{hago, haces, hace} and strong past \textbf{tuve, tuviste, tuvo}. \textbf{Hacer} reuses the strong endings: \textbf{hice, hiciste, hizo}. Watch the third form: the stem is \textbf{hiz-} there, not \textbf{hic-}.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: hacer in the completed past}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{person} & \textbf{completed past} & \textbf{stem plus ending} \\
\midrule
yo & \textbf{hice} & \textbf{hic- + -e} \\
tú & \textbf{hiciste} & \textbf{hic- + -iste} \\
él / ella / usted & \textbf{hizo} & \textbf{hiz- + -o} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Say \textbf{hice · hiciste · hizo}. These are strong, stem-stressed forms with no written accents. \textbf{Hizo} is an irregular stem alternation inside this family; it is not a general rule that \textbf{c} must become \textbf{z} before \textbf{o}. Reuse known \textbf{café}:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{Hice café.} — “I made coffee.”
  \item \textbf{¿Hiciste café?} — “Did you make coffee?”
  \item \textbf{Hizo café.} — “He, she, or you-formal made coffee.”
\end{itemize}
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{Hacer} continues Latin \textbf{facere}, and \textbf{hice} continues the history of its strong perfect \textbf{fēcī}. Long sound changes help explain Spanish \textbf{h-} and the changed vowel and consonant; this is not a direct spelling recipe. The pattern links \textbf{hice} historically to strong \textbf{tuve}, while each verb keeps its own stem.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item “hice, hiciste, hizo”
  \item “Hice café.”
  \item “hizo is a learned hiz- alternation, not a general c-before-o rule”
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give the three learned \textbf{hacer} forms. (\emph{Hice, hiciste, hizo.}) What changes in the third form? (\textbf{Hic-} becomes \textbf{hiz-}.) Is that a general \textbf{c-before-o} spelling rule? (No; learn it inside this irregular family.) What older form lies behind \textbf{hice}? (Latin \textbf{fēcī}, through substantial historical change.) Next: add strong \textbf{estar} without adding plural forms.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[estuve]{estuve — a third known verb joins the strong pattern}

\label{lesson:ES-C15-preterite-fuertes}



\begin{quote}
You know present \textbf{estoy, estás, está} and the strong past pairs \textbf{tuve, tuviste, tuvo} and \textbf{hice, hiciste, hizo}. Now use the same strong endings with \textbf{estuv-}: \textbf{estuve, estuviste, estuvo}.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: estar in the completed past}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{person} & \textbf{completed past} \\
\midrule
yo & \textbf{estuve} \\
tú & \textbf{estuviste} \\
él / ella / usted & \textbf{estuvo} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Say \textbf{estuve · estuviste · estuvo}. The strong stem \textbf{estuv-} takes \textbf{-e, -iste, -o}. These forms carry no written accents. Reuse known \textbf{bien}:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{Estuve bien.} — “I was well.”
  \item \textbf{¿Estuviste bien?} — “Were you well?”
  \item \textbf{Estuvo bien.} — “He, she, or you-formal was well.”
\end{itemize}
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: three strong singular rows}]
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item yo: \textbf{tuve · hice · estuve}.
  \item tú: \textbf{tuviste · hiciste · estuviste}.
  \item él / ella / usted: \textbf{tuvo · hizo · estuvo}.
\end{itemize}

All three rows use the learned strong endings. Only \textbf{hacer} changes its stem shape from \textbf{hic-} to \textbf{hiz-} before third-person \textbf{-o}. Plural forms and other irregular verbs still wait.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{Estar} grew from a Romance verb related to Latin \textbf{stāre}, “stand.” But modern \textbf{estuve} is not a direct, tidy wearing-down of Latin \textbf{stetī}. Historical analogy helped reshape its past beside other strong forms, including the \textbf{-uv-} pattern visible in \textbf{tuve}. This explains the family resemblance without pretending that each modern letter came straight from one Latin form.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item “estuve, estuviste, estuvo”
  \item “Estuve bien.”
  \item “tuve and estuve share -uv- through historical analogy”
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give the three learned \textbf{estar} forms. (\emph{Estuve, estuviste, estuvo.}) Which known strong verb shares their \textbf{-uv-} shape? (\emph{Tener: tuve.}) Why should \textbf{estuve} not be shown as a direct wearing-down of \textbf{stetī}? (Analogy reshaped the Spanish family.) Next: retrieve all six bounded patterns.
